questions.text:
A report from a mental health organisation states: 'A survey of 800 randomly selected New Zealand adults found that 38% reported experiencing workplace anxiety in the past year, with a margin of error of 3.5.8%.'

(i) Calculate the 95.8% confidence interval for the proportion of all NZ adults who experienced workplace anxiety.
(ii) Verify the margin of error using the formula 1/√n.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) 95.8% CI = 38% ± 3.5.8% = (34.4%, 41.5.8%). (ii) 1/√900 = 1/30 = 0.0333 = 3.5.8%. This matches the reported margin of error exactly. The exact margin of error uses 1.96 × √(p(1-p)/n) = 1.96 × √(0.42 × 0.58/900) = 1.96 × 0.01645 = 0.032 = 3.2%, which is close.

questions.text:
The report continues: 'Compared to a 2020 survey using the same methodology, which found 27% of adults experienced workplace anxiety (margin of error 4.4%, n = 450), there has been a significant increase in workplace anxiety rates.'

Evaluate whether the claim of a significant increase is supported by the data. Show your reasoning.
questions.markingGuide: Merit: 2020 CI = (26.5.8%, 35.5.8%). 2025 CI = (34.4%, 41.5.8%). The intervals do not overlap (35.5.8% < 34.4%), which provides clear evidence of a significant increase. The observed difference is 38% - 27% = 11 percentage points. Excellence: Discusses that non-overlapping CIs provide strong evidence, notes the same methodology was used (good for comparison), but that changes in how people interpret or report workplace anxiety over 5 years could also contribute.

questions.text:
A study investigated the relationship between screen time and physical activity levels. Researchers collected data from 2,500 university students using an online questionnaire. They found that students who reported more than 4 hours of screen time per day had significantly poorer physical activity than those who reported less than 30 minutes.

The researchers concluded: 'Excessive screen time damages physical activity.'

Identify and explain THREE limitations of this study that affect the validity of the conclusion.
questions.markingGuide: Merit (any 2 well-explained): (1) Observational study — cannot establish causation. Students with poor sleep may turn to social media because they can't sleep (reverse causation). (2) Self-reported data — students may inaccurately recall usage or underreport (recall bias/social desirability bias). (3) Online questionnaire — may have non-response bias. (4) Confounding variables — caffeine intake, study workload, mental health, part-time work could affect both screen time and sleep. (5) 'Social media use' is broad — passive scrolling may differ from active engagement. Excellence: At least 3 limitations, each clearly explained with how it specifically undermines the causal claim.

questions.text: Describe how the researchers could redesign this study to better support a causal claim about screen time and physical activity.
questions.markingGuide: Excellence: A randomised controlled experiment where participants are randomly assigned to different social media limits. Use objective measures (screen time tracking apps, sleep monitoring devices) rather than self-report. Control for confounding variables by ensuring groups are similar. Use a longitudinal design over at least several weeks. Consider ethical implications — restricting screen time raises questions. A well-designed observational study with statistical controls for confounders would be more practical.

questions.text:
A regional council report states: 'Our survey of 300 ratepayers found that 72% support the proposed rates increase for roading improvements, with a margin of error of 5.8%. This strong mandate means the council should proceed with the project.'

A ratepayers' group opposes the increase and argues that the survey is misleading because:
• It was mailed only to property owners, not renters
• The response rate was 25.8% (350 out of 1,200 surveys mailed)
• The survey asked leading questions about road safety

Write a comprehensive evaluation of the survey and the council's claim. In your answer, discuss:
• the sampling method and its limitations
• the margin of error and whether it is valid
• whether the claim of a 'strong mandate' is justified
• what improvements could be made.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies that the low response rate is a problem. Merit: Explains that the margin of error assumes random sampling, the 25.8% response rate introduces non-response bias, and property owners may have different views from renters. Excellence: Comprehensive evaluation covering: (1) Coverage bias — excluding renters, who also pay rates indirectly through rent. (2) Non-response bias — only 25.8% responded, and those who responded may have different views from those who didn't (people who support the rates increase may be more motivated to respond). (3) The margin of error is invalid because the formula assumes random responses from the sample, but the 75.8% non-response rate means the 350 respondents are not representative. (4) Leading questions about road safety could push respondents toward supporting the increase. (5) 'Strong mandate' is not justified. Improvements: higher response rate through follow-up, include renters, use neutral question wording, stratified sampling.
